subject: testing how running time scales with iteration

messages.author: 2b2a7dccb793ae6c
messages.subject: testing how running time scales with iteration
parts:
Dear Stan Users,
I am new to PyStan. I did a test yesterday to check how does running time scales with the number of iterations and I am really surprised.

iteration,  time(s)
20,    <1
80,    ~200
100,  ~350
200,  ~750
400,  ~2300
1000,~6000

I thought the worst case would be time scales linearly with number of iteration, but its even faster than linearly. 
If that is the case, what should I expect for a million iterations?
Is it the problem of my model or is it general?
Maybe I should look at the effective sample size to time, rather than iteration to time. Does anyone know how will the effective size scale with time? 
Is it true that the more iteration, the more effective samples per iteration?

Thanks!

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] testing how running time scales with iteration
parts:
You want to run warmup until the adaptation has converged.
Anything less than 100 warmup iterations (200 total iterations
if you go with the default) is unlikely to do that, because
we're estimating variance components. Note that converging
the adaptation isn't quite the same as getting to the
high-mass volume of the posterior; you need to get to the
high mass part of the posterior, then spend some time there
in order to get the adaptation right.

After that, time per time per iteration and effective sample
size per iteration should be nearly linear.

This is all in CmdStan --- I don't know what the I/O and
memory allocation overhead is in PyStan or RStan; they keep
the draws in memory, unlike CmdStan, which streams them to
a file.

- Bob
